The symmetric difference keeps the edges in exactly one graph, A–C and C–D; the shared edges are dashed and node B, left with no edges, is dropped." width="100%"} Returns a new graph containing edges that are in exactly one of the two graphs. Equivalent to `(G1 - G2) ∪ (G2 - G1)`. Edges are matched by their endpoint node IDs (in the same direction, for directed graphs), regardless of weights or attributes. The result is everything that differs between the two graphs, with the shared part removed, which makes it useful for: - surveying all changes between two snapshots of a network in a single graph - measuring how far apart two networks are (e.g., the number of edges in the result is the edge-edit distance between two graphs on the same node IDs) - highlighting disagreement between two inferred or reported networks Nodes are matched by ID, so both graphs must use the same numbering for the same entities. Only endpoints of the remaining edges are kept. Each remaining edge keeps the weight and attributes from the graph it came from. The result does not record which graph an edge came from; call `difference()` in each direction when you need to distinguish additions from removals. Edges from this graph keep their IDs; edges from `other` get fresh IDs above every ID this graph has used. Neither input graph is modified. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [other]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The graph to compare with. It must have the same directedness as this graph. Its edges that this graph lacks are included in the result with their own weights and attributes; for nodes, this graph's labels and attributes win and `other` fills in what is missing. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new graph containing edges in exactly one of the graphs, plus their endpoints. It is weighted if either input is weighted. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graphs have different directedness, or if the same label belongs to different node IDs among the nodes kept from the two graphs. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Symmetric difference keeps edges present in exactly one of the two graphs, dropping any node that ends up edge-isolated. Unlike `difference()` it is symmetric: the same set comes back regardless of which graph makes the call. Both operands must agree on directedness. Each surviving edge keeps the weight and attributes it had in its own graph; node attributes are merged, with the calling graph winning ties. This is the go-to operation for surveying all changes between two network snapshots without having to reason about direction. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Edges `1-2` and `2-3` are shared by both graphs and drop out, leaving only the triangle's closing edge `3-1`, which exists in just one of them: ::: {#4b6098a1 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec # Triangle g1 = ec.Graph(directed=False) for i in range(1, 4): g1.add_node() g1.add_edges([(1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 1)]) # Path g2 = ec.Graph(directed=False) for i in range(1, 4): g2.add_node() g2.add_edges([(1, 2), (2, 3)]) sym_diff = g1.symmetric_difference(g2) sym_diff.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 1 ``` ::: ::: Unlike `difference()`, this is symmetric, which makes it well-suited for spotting everything that changed between two network snapshots, regardless of which direction the change went. Between these two yearly snapshots of a friendship network, one friendship ended ("Cat"-"Dan") and one formed ("Ann"-"Cat"): ::: {#ae340391 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} def snapshot(friendships): g = ec.Graph(directed=False) g.add_nodes(["Ann", "Bob", "Cat", "Dan", "Eve"]) g.add_edges(friendships) return g year1 = snapshot([("Ann", "Bob"), ("Bob", "Cat"), ("Cat", "Dan"), ("Dan", "Eve")]) year2 = snapshot([("Ann", "Bob"), ("Bob", "Cat"), ("Ann", "Cat"), ("Dan", "Eve")]) changes = year1.symmetric_difference(year2) changes.get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ['Cat--Dan', 'Ann--Cat'] ``` ::: ::: Calling it from the other graph gives the same set of edges: ::: {#58b7ec89 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} sorted(year2.symmetric_difference(year1).get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` ['Ann--Cat', 'Cat--Dan'] ``` ::: :::
